sn12.15:1.1: This discourse was quoted by Ānanda to Channa at [sn22.90:9.1](). It was cited by name in Nāgārjuna’s Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 15.7: “In the Advice to Kātyāyana, both ‘exists’ and ‘does not exist’ are denied by the Buddha, expert in being and non-being.” Nāgārjuna’s text, an important Buddhist philosophical treatise, is studied extensively to this day.
sn12.15:1.4: Right view is normally defined as understanding the four noble truths ([dn22:21.4](), [mn141:24.1](), [sn45.8:3.1]()).
sn12.15:2.1: The Buddha refers to a widely held belief which can be traced to the prominent Vedic saying: “This is twofold, there is no third: truth and falsehood. The gods are truth, humans are falsehood.” (_Dvayaṁ vā idaṁ na tṛtīyamasti: satyaṁ caivānṛtaṁ ca. Satyameva devā anṛtam manuṣyā_, Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.1.1.4, 3.3.2.2, 3.9.4.1). The word for “truth” here is _satya_ (Pali _sacca_), which like _atthitā_ (“existence”) is an abstract noun from the root _as_, “to exist”. The word for “falsehood” is _anṛta_, a form not used in this sense in Pali, which uses the simple negative. The gods are truly real because they are immortal, whereas transient humans are not truly real. _Satya_ and _anṛta_ are a standard pair in pre-Buddhist Sanskrit, harking back to Rig Veda 7.49.3. Consider also the hymn of creation at Arthavaveda 10.2.14: “Who placed truth in him, who falsehood, who mortality, who immortality?”
